{{Short description|Correlation coefficient used when one variable is dichotomous}}
The '''point biserial correlation coefficient''' (''r<sub>pb</sub>'') is a [[correlation coefficient]] used when one variable (e.g. ''Y'') is [[dichotomy|dichotomous]]; ''Y'' can either be "naturally" dichotomous, like whether a coin lands heads or tails, or an artificially dichotomized variable. In most situations it is not advisable to dichotomize variables artificially.<ref>{{cite journal |last=MacCallum |first=Robert C. |display-authors=1 |last2=Zhang |first2=Shaobo |last3=Preacher |first3=Kristopher J. |last4=Rucker |first4=Derek D. |year=2002 |title=On the Practice of Dichotomization of Quantitative Variables |journal=Psychological Methods |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=19–40 |doi=10.1037/1082-989X.7.1.19 |hdl=1808/1495 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> When a new variable is artificially dichotomized the new dichotomous variable may be conceptualized as having an underlying continuity. If this is the case, a [[biserial correlation]] would be the more appropriate calculation.

The point-biserial correlation is mathematically equivalent to the [[Pearson correlation coefficient|Pearson (product moment) correlation coefficient]]; that is, if we have one continuously measured variable ''X'' and a dichotomous variable ''Y'', ''r<sub>XY</sub>'' = ''r<sub>pb</sub>''. This can be shown by assigning two distinct numerical values to the dichotomous variable.

__TOC__
==Calculation==

To calculate ''r<sub>pb</sub>'', assume that the dichotomous variable ''Y'' has the two values 0 and 1. If we divide the [[data set]] into two groups, group 1 which received the value "1" on ''Y'' and group 2 which received the value "0" on ''Y'', then the point-biserial correlation coefficient is calculated as follows:
:<math>
r_{pb} = \frac{M_1 - M_0}{s_n} \sqrt{ \frac{n_1 n_0}{n^2}},
</math>
where ''s<sub>n</sub>'' is the [[standard deviation]] used when data are available for every member of the population:
<br>
:<math>s_n = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline{X})^2}\,,</math>
''M''<sub>1</sub> being the mean value on the continuous variable ''X'' for all data points in group 1, and ''M''<sub>0</sub> the mean value on the continuous variable ''X'' for all data points in group 2.  Further, ''n''<sub>1</sub> is the number of data points in group 1, ''n''<sub>0</sub> is the number of data points in group 2 and ''n'' is the total sample size.  This formula is a computational formula that has been derived from the formula for ''r<sub>XY</sub>'' in order to reduce steps in the calculation; it is easier to compute than ''r<sub>XY</sub>''.

There is an equivalent formula that uses ''s''<sub>''n''−1</sub>:

:<math>
r_{pb} = \frac{M_1 - M_0}{s_{n-1}} \sqrt{ \frac{n_1 n_0}{n(n-1)}},
</math>

where ''s''<sub>''n''−1</sub> is the standard deviation used when data are available only for a sample of the population:

:<math>s_{n-1} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline{X})^2}.</math>

The version of the formula using ''s''<sub>''n''−1</sub> is useful if one is calculating point-biserial correlation coefficients in a programming language or other development environment where there is a function available for calculating ''s''<sub>''n''−1</sub>, but no function available for calculating ''s<sub>n</sub>''.<ref>A correct version of point biserial formula can be found in {{Cite book
 | first = Gene V. |last=Glass |first2=Kenneth D. |last2=Hopkins
 | title = Statistical Methods in Education and Psychology
 | edition = 3rd
 | publisher = [[Allyn & Bacon]]
 | year = 1995
 | isbn = 0-205-14212-5
 | url-access = registration
 | url = https://archive.org/details/statisticalmetho00glas
 }}</ref>

Also the square of the point biserial correlation coefficient can be written:
:<math>
\frac{ (M_1 - M_0)^2} {\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline{X})^2} \left( \frac{n_1 n_0}{n} \right)\,.
</math>

We can test the [[null hypothesis]] that the correlation is zero in the population.  A little algebra shows that the usual formula for assessing the significance of a correlation coefficient, when applied to ''r<sub>pb</sub>'', is the same as the formula for an unpaired [[Student's t-test|''t''-test]] and so

:<math>
r_{pb} \sqrt{ \frac{n_1+n_0-2}{1-r_{pb}^2}}
</math>

follows [[Student's t-distribution]] with (''n''<sub>1</sub>+''n''<sub>0</sub> − 2) degrees of freedom when the null hypothesis is true.

One disadvantage of the point biserial coefficient is that the further the distribution of ''Y'' is from 50/50, the more constrained will be the range of values which the coefficient can take.  If it can be assumed that the dichotomous variable ''Y'' is normally distributed, a better descriptive index is given by the [[Biserial correlation|biserial coefficient]]:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Sheskin |first1=David J. |title=Handbook of parametric and nonparametric statistical procedures |date=2011 |publisher=CRC Press, Taylor & Francis Group |location=Boca Raton London New York |isbn=978-1-4398-5801-1 |page=1329 |edition=Fifth}}</ref>

:<math>
r_{b} = \frac{M_1 - M_0}{s_{n-1}} \frac{n_1 n_0}{n^2\phi\left(\Phi^{-1}\left(n_1/n\right)\right)} \sqrt{\frac{n}{n-1}},
</math>

where <math>\phi</math> is the [[Probability density function|density]] of the [[normal distribution]] with zero mean and unit variance and <math>\Phi^{-1}</math> is its [[quantile function|inverse CDF]].  This is not easy to calculate, and the biserial coefficient is not widely used in practice.

A specific case of biserial correlation occurs where ''X'' is the sum of a number of dichotomous variables of which ''Y'' is one.  An example of this is where ''X''  is a person's total score on a test composed of ''n'' dichotomously scored items.  A statistic of interest (which is a discrimination index) is the correlation between responses to a given item and the corresponding total test scores.  There are three computations in wide use,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Linacre |first=John |title=The Expected Value of a Point-Biserial (or Similar) Correlation |journal=Rasch Measurement Transactions |volume=22 |year=2008 |issue=1 |page=1154 |url=http://www.rasch.org/rmt/rmt221e.htm}}</ref> all called the ''point-biserial correlation'': (i) the Pearson correlation between item scores and total test scores including the item scores, (ii) the Pearson correlation between item scores and total test scores excluding the item scores, and (iii) a correlation adjusted for the bias caused by the inclusion of item scores in the test scores. Correlation (iii) is

:<math>
r_{upb}=\frac{M_1-M_0-1}{\sqrt{\frac{n^2s_n^2}{n_1n_0}-2(M_1-M_0)+1}}.
</math>

A slightly different version of the point biserial coefficient is the rank biserial which occurs where the variable ''X'' consists of ranks while ''Y'' is dichotomous.  We could calculate the coefficient in the same way as where ''X'' is continuous but it would have the same disadvantage that the range of values it can take on becomes more constrained as the distribution of ''Y'' becomes more unequal.  To get round this, we note that the coefficient will have its largest value where the smallest ranks are all opposite the 0s and the largest ranks are opposite the 1s.  Its smallest value occurs where the reverse is the case.  These values are respectively plus and minus (''n''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''n''<sub>0</sub>)/2.  We can therefore use the reciprocal of this value to rescale the difference between the observed mean ranks on to the interval from plus one to minus one.  The result is

:<math>
r_{rb} = 2\frac{M_1 - M_0}{n_1+n_0},
</math>

where ''M''<sub>1</sub> and ''M''<sub>0</sub> are respectively the means of the ranks corresponding to the 1 and 0 scores of the dichotomous variable. This formula, which simplifies the calculation from the counting of agreements and inversions, is due to Gene V Glass (1966).

It is possible to use this to test the null hypothesis of zero correlation in the population from which the sample was drawn.  If ''r<sub>rb</sub>'' is calculated as above then the smaller of

:<math>
(1+r_{rb})\frac{n_1n_0}{2}
</math>

and

:<math>
(1-r_{rb})\frac{n_1n_0}{2}
</math>

is distributed as [[Mann–Whitney U]] with sample sizes ''n''<sub>1</sub> and ''n''<sub>0</sub> when the null hypothesis is true.
